title: Cum clauses

objectives.can: Tell the preposition cum from the conjunction, and read cum with the subjunctive as 'when', 'since' or 'although'.

explanation.summary: *cum* is two different words: a preposition meaning 'with', and a conjunction that begins a clause meaning 'when', 'since' or 'although'. With the indicative it states a time. With the subjunctive it gives the circumstances of the main action, and it is one of the commonest clauses in Gospel narrative.

sections.heading: The preposition and the conjunction
body: The preposition *cum* takes the ablative and means 'with': *qui erant cum Jesu* (Matthew 26:51), 'who were with Jesus'. It does not begin a clause and there is no verb of its own. With a personal pronoun it is written after the pronoun, as one word: *vobiscum* ('with you'), *nobiscum* ('with us').

The conjunction *cum* begins a subordinate clause that has its own verb and subject, usually with a nominative subject and a finite verb: *cum introisset Capharnaum* (Matthew 8:5), 'when he had entered Capernaum'. The test is simple. If the next words are a noun or pronoun in the ablative and no verb, it is the preposition. If a verb follows soon with its own subject, it is the conjunction.

sections.heading: Cum with the indicative: a time
body: When *cum* simply says when something happens or happened, it takes the indicative. In Matthew 6:5 the clause *Et cum oratis* means 'and whenever you pray': a present indicative describes what is going on or happens regularly. In Matthew 9:15 *Venient autem dies cum auferetur ab eis sponsus*, 'the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them', the verb is a future indicative.

John 16:21 puts two time clauses side by side. *cum parit* uses a present indicative ('when she is giving birth'), and *cum autem pepererit* uses a future perfect for an action that will be complete before the main verb ('when she has given birth').

sections.heading: Cum with the subjunctive: the circumstances
body: In narrative about the past *cum* usually takes the subjunctive: the imperfect for an action that was going on and the pluperfect for an action that was finished before the main action. John 19:23 reads *Milites ergo cum crucifixissent eum, acceperunt vestimenta ejus*: 'when the soldiers had crucified him, they took his clothes'. The pluperfect subjunctive *crucifixissent* shows that the crucifixion was complete. John 8:7 has the imperfect: *Cum ergo perseverarent interrogantes eum*, 'when they kept on questioning him'.

The English may be 'when', 'after' or 'as', and the clause is often translated by a participle ('having crucified him'). What it does is set the scene for the main verb. The pattern *cum autem venisset* is the opening of many Gospel scenes, and you will read it dozens of times.
The subjunctive here is a feature of the construction and does not mean 'might'. Translate it as an ordinary past tense.

sections.heading: Cum meaning 'since' or 'although'
body: The same *cum* with the subjunctive can also give a reason ('since') or a concession ('although'). The context decides. Romans 1:21 says *Quia cum cognovissent Deum, non sicut Deum glorificaverunt*: although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God. The clause states something that would lead us to expect the opposite of what the main verb says. In John 12:37 the same idea appears: *Cum autem tanta signa fecisset coram eis, non credebant in eum*, 'although he had done so many signs before them, they did not believe in him'.

John 21:11 has a present-time example in the imperfect: *Et cum tanti essent, non est scissum rete*, 'and although there were so many, the net was not torn'. A reason and a concession can look alike in form. Ask whether the clause explains the main verb ('since') or stands against it ('although').

Mood
Meaning
Example
rows: when, after, as (circumstance in the past)

sections.heading: Other words for 'when', 'before' and 'until'
body: *postquam* ('after') normally takes the indicative: *Postquam ergo lavit pedes eorum* (John 13:12), 'after he had washed their feet'. *dum* ('while') also takes the indicative in John 12:35, *dum lucem habetis*, 'while you have the light'.

*antequam* and *priusquam* ('before') often take the subjunctive when the thing has not yet happened or is a limit: *antequam Abraham fieret* (John 8:58), *priusquam in utero conciperetur* (Luke 2:21), 'before he was conceived in the womb'. *donec* ('until') takes the subjunctive in Matthew 5:18, *donec transeat cælum et terra*, 'until heaven and earth pass away', where the end is expected but has not come. These words are met in the later lessons of this stage, so treat them here as a brief look.

misunderstandings: Translating every *cum* as 'with'. Look for a verb in the clause: if there is one, it is the conjunction.
Reading the subjunctive after *cum* as 'might' or 'may'. In narrative it is an ordinary past circumstance.
Taking a pluperfect subjunctive as 'would have'. In *cum venisset* it means 'when he had come'. 'Would have' belongs to conditional sentences, a later lesson.
Deciding 'since' or 'although' from the form alone. Only the context shows whether the clause explains the main verb or runs against it.

deeper.heading: Why the subjunctive in narrative?
body: Early Latin put the indicative after *cum* in a past narrative, and the subjunctive spread in classical prose until it became the usual form for a clause that gives circumstances. The Vulgate follows the later usage. For a learner the practical rule is enough: *cum* with an imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive in a story is the circumstances.

reading.why: Three *cum* clauses with a pluperfect subjunctive in eight verses (the soldiers, Jesus seeing his mother, Jesus receiving the vinegar), each setting the scene for a main verb. Notice how the narrative moves from one finished action to the next.
